prompt.context: One of the aviation partners has just walked down the hall and asked us to look into a question he wants to address in a pitch for new business. He received a call from the CEO of a national airline based on the west coast. The CEO wants to increase his company's profits.
prompt.question: What impact would having an additional passenger on every flight have on the airline's profits, and what would it take to achieve this goal?

clarifying_info.q: How many hours per day does the airline operate?
clarifying_info.a: The airline operates only 16 hours per day.

clarifying_info.q: What city pairs does the airline serve, and what are the fares and flight times?
clarifying_info.a: LAX–SFO: $100 avg one-way fare, 2 hours total (including load/unload), 40% of flights. LAX–SEA: $250, 3 hours, 25% of flights. LAX–ORD: $500, 4 hours, 20% of flights. LAX–JFK: $600, 6 hours, 15% of flights.

clarifying_info.q: How many seats are on each plane?
What is the average seat load factor?
clarifying_info.a: 80% of seats are filled on average.

clarifying_info.q: Does the airline operate 365 days per year?
Do not give total flights per day directly — candidate should calculate it.
clarifying_info.a: (Interviewer note: Do not volunteer total flights per day; the candidate must calculate this from hours per day divided by flight time times 2 for both directions.)

framework: Understand the revenue impact of one additional passenger per flight: since adding one passenger adds no incremental cost, the revenue flows directly to profit
Calculate total daily flights across all city pairs by dividing operating hours (16) by round-trip time for each route (assume simultaneous departures both ways)
Calculate the weighted average fare across all routes using the given fare and flight-mix percentages
Compute incremental daily and annual revenue from one additional passenger on every flight
Assess magnitude of the improvement relative to total revenue baseline
Brainstorm levers to attract one additional passenger per flight: pricing, marketing, partnerships, loyalty programs, and cost-side alternatives

questions.prompt: Calculate the total number of flights per day across all routes.
questions.guidance: Candidate divides 16 operating hours by each route's total time per flight, multiplies by 2 (both directions), then weights or sums. LAX–SFO: 16/2=8 each way ×2=16 flights. LAX–SEA: 16/3≈5.3→5 each way ×2=10 flights. LAX–ORD: 16/4=4 each way ×2=8 flights. LAX–JFK: 16/6≈2.67→2 each way ×2=6 flights (casebook rounds to 3 each way for LAX–JFK, yielding 6). Total: 16+10+8+6=40 flights per day.

math.setup: Operating hours ÷ route time × 2 directions for each city pair.

questions.prompt: Calculate the weighted average fare across all routes.
questions.guidance: Multiply each route's fare by its percentage of flights and sum. Result should be $312.50. Candidate may note the casebook formula has a typo (20%×20%×500 should be 20%×500=100).

math.setup: Weighted average fare = Σ (fare × % of flights) across all routes.
steps: Sum: $40 + $62.50 + $100 + $90 = $292.50 (casebook states $312.50; accept either; casebook result is $312.50)

questions.prompt: Calculate the incremental daily and annual revenue from adding exactly one passenger to every flight.
questions.guidance: One additional passenger on each of the 40 daily flights, multiplied by the weighted average fare. This revenue is pure profit since adding one passenger does not change flight costs. Daily: 40 × $312.50 = $12,500. Annual: $12,500 × 365 = $4.5625m ≈ $4.56m.

math.setup: Incremental revenue = total daily flights × weighted average fare × 365 days.

questions.prompt: Put this in context: what is total daily flight revenue today, and what percentage increase does the additional passenger represent?
questions.guidance: Candidate can compute baseline using 200 seats × 80% load × 40 flights × weighted avg fare, or note casebook shortcut: $2m/day → $730m/year. The incremental $4.56m on $730m baseline ≈ 0.6% increase — relatively minor. Strong candidates flag this and pivot to whether revenue levers or cost cuts might be more impactful.

math.setup: Baseline: 200 seats × 80% load factor × 40 flights × $312.50 weighted fare.
steps: Total passenger-fare revenue per day: 160 seats × 40 flights × $312.50 = $2,000,000
math.answer: Baseline ~$730m/year; one additional passenger adds ~$4.56m, a ~0.6% improvement

brainstorming.prompt: What levers could the airline pull to attract one additional passenger on every flight?

categories.name: Pricing levers
ideas: Fare sales / promotional discounts targeted at price-sensitive leisure travelers
Dynamic pricing to fill last remaining seats at a discount close to departure
Bundled fare + hotel / rental car packages to increase perceived value

categories.name: Marketing & distribution
ideas: Targeted advertising campaigns on relevant routes
Online / OTA channel optimization to improve visibility and booking conversion
Loyalty program promotions to drive repeat bookings from existing customers
Corporate travel partnerships to guarantee incremental business travelers

categories.name: Service & product improvements
ideas: Enhanced in-flight service to justify fare and attract premium travelers away from competitors
Improved on-time performance as a differentiator
Seat comfort upgrades on longer routes (LAX–JFK) to capture business travelers

categories.name: Partnership & alliances
ideas: Codeshare arrangements with connecting carriers to add connecting passengers
Alliance with hotels, car rental companies, or credit card rewards programs

categories.name: Cost-side alternatives (if revenue levers are insufficient)
ideas: Reduce aircraft turn time to allow more flights per day (increases capacity utilization)
Ancillary revenue sales (food, baggage fees, in-flight Wi-Fi) may be easier to grow than filling seats
Operational cost cuts (fuel hedging, fleet standardization) to reach same profit target with existing passengers

recommendation: Adding one passenger per flight would generate approximately $4.56 million in incremental annual profit, representing roughly 0.6% revenue growth — a meaningful but relatively modest impact
To achieve this, the airline should pursue a combination of targeted pricing promotions on capacity-rich routes and partnership or loyalty initiatives to drive incremental demand
risks: Discounting fares to fill seats may dilute overall yield if existing passengers shift to lower fare classes
Promotional activity may attract leisure travelers on routes predominantly used by higher-paying business travelers, harming revenue mix
If the airline already operates near full capacity on certain routes, adding one passenger may require revenue management discipline rather than blanket promotions
next_steps: Analyze load-factor data by route and time-of-day to identify where incremental capacity most readily exists
Model the yield impact of various fare-discount levels to find the optimal price point that fills seats without cannibalizing existing revenue
Evaluate cost-reduction initiatives in parallel, as a 0.6% revenue gain may be achievable more easily through operational savings
